about: Black holes with a star going round them, found from the wobble Gaia measured in the star's path across the sky, then confirmed by the star's changing speed towards and away from us. None is feeding: nothing has been seen falling in, so they give off no light of their own. Each is found only by what it pulls on.
drawn: The star on its measured orbit at the clock's date. Both go round their shared centre of mass: the black hole, many times heavier, swings round a small loop of its own. The black hole's shadow is drawn at its true size, with the light from behind bent round it. The system stays where Gaia measured it (it really drifts across the sky, as the stars do, which aren't moved either).
about_fed: Black holes fed by the star going round them: gas from the star spirals into a disc round the black hole and heats up as it falls, the inner disc to millions of degrees, shining in X-rays. Some of it is flung out along the black hole's spin axis as jets, seen in radio.
drawn_fed: The star on its measured orbit at the clock's date, its shape the space where its own gravity rules (the black hole's pull stretches it), darker where its surface gravity is weaker. The disc at the temperatures disc theory gives for its measured feeding rate (a quiet disc's: the one temperature that gives its measured share of the light; GRS 1915+105's outer disc warmed by its own X-rays, as much as gives its measured share of the infrared), in the orbit's plane (MAXI J1820+070's spin is tilted from it), as the eye would see it up close, hotter and brighter on the side coming towards you, broken into the patches and rings its turbulence makes (the pattern ours: patches the size simulations give, each lasting about an orbit, carried round and sheared by the gas's motion, slowed to at most one inner orbit a second), its edges thinning out to see-through (ours: their profile isn't measured); its light, the star's and the sky's bent round the spinning black hole along the exact paths light takes there. Where a radio jet has been seen resolved, a line marks its direction (the jet itself isn't visible to the eye). Where the orbit's tilt, its turn on our sky, the spin or where the star is along its orbit now isn't measured, the card says what's drawn instead. The system stays where it was measured (it really drifts across the sky, as the stars do).
about_lone: A black hole alone, with no star going round it, found only because it passed in front of a more distant star and bent its light (gravitational microlensing). The Milky Way should hold about a hundred million black holes made by stars, most of them alone and dark like this one.
drawn_lone: Its shadow at its true size, with the light from behind bent round it; its spin isn't known, so it's drawn not spinning. Seen from Earth's side, looking past it at the stars it passed in front of; the star it lensed, 18,000 light-years farther and far too faint, isn't drawn. The black hole stays where it was in 2011 (it really drifts across the sky, 6 thousandths of an arcsecond a year). The chart shows the event as seen from Earth at the clock's date: how bright the star looked, and where its two images were.
about_cluster: A black hole between the two kinds known for sure: heavier than any made by a single star (up to about 100 Suns), far lighter than the giants at galaxies' centres (Sgr A*: 4 million Suns). Such medium-sized black holes may be what the giants grew from, but they're hard to find: they sit quietly at the hearts of star clusters, seen only by how they pull on the stars round them.
drawn_cluster: The black hole at the cluster's centre as measured (Anderson & van der Marel 2010; its true place is within about an arcsecond of it), its shadow at its true size for 40,000 Suns, with the light from behind bent round it; its spin isn't known, so it's drawn not spinning. The seven fast stars at their measured places in 2012, moving across the sky as measured over 2002-2023, in straight lines (bound to the black hole they'd curve: centuries from now their drawn places are off). How far each is in front of or behind the black hole isn't known: drawn from the spread the discoverers assumed (0.022 parsecs), as near as it must be to stay bound; their speeds towards or away from us aren't known either (drawn as none). Their colours and brightness from Hubble's two colours. The cluster's other stars round them are Gaia's (it misses most of the crowded core).

systems.name: Gaia BH1
systems.title: Dormant black hole with a Sun-like star
systems.about: Found in 2022 from the wobble of a Sun-like star in Gaia's measurements: then the nearest known black hole, three times closer than any other. The star swings round it on a wide oval, far too wide for the star's gas to spill onto it, so it isn't feeding: Chandra and the VLA saw no X-rays or radio from it.

Rodriguez et al. 2024, PASP 136, 024203 (no X-rays or radio)

systems.name: Gaia BH2
systems.title: Dormant black hole with a red giant
systems.about: Found in 2023, also from Gaia's measurements: a red giant (a star like the Sun near the end of its life, swollen to about 8 times its width) going round a black hole of about 9 Suns every 3.5 years. Even at its closest the giant is far too small to spill gas onto it, and no X-rays or radio were seen from it near its closest approach.
refs: El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 521, 4323 (Table 2: the joint Gaia + RV fit; RVs: their Table 1)
Rodriguez et al. 2024, PASP 136, 024203 (no X-rays or radio)

systems.name: Gaia BH3
systems.title: Dormant black hole with an ancient giant
systems.about: Found in 2024 while checking data for Gaia's fourth release: about 33 Suns, then the most massive black hole of a star known in the Milky Way. Its star is one of the oldest kind, a giant with under 1/300 of the Sun's share of metals, from the halo: probably once in a small star cluster that the Milky Way tore apart (the ED-2 stream). They go round each other every 11.6 years on a long ellipse. Chandra saw no X-rays from it.
refs: Gaia Collaboration, Panuzzo et al. 2024, A&A 686, L2 (Table 2: the combined solution; Table 3: the star; RVs: Table C.1)
Cappelluti et al. 2024, ApJ 973, 75 (no X-rays)

systems.name: Cygnus X-1
systems.title: Black hole fed by a blue supergiant
systems.about: One of the first X-ray sources found (1964), and in 1972 the first object most astronomers accepted as a black hole, from the orbit of its star. The star, a blue supergiant 40 times the Sun's mass, nearly fills the space where its own gravity rules. The black hole draws in its fierce wind, which settles into a disc of gas millions of degrees hot, and it spins nearly as fast as anything can.

systems.name: V404 Cygni
systems.title: Flaring black hole fed by a swollen orange star
systems.about: Flared in 1938 and again in 1989, when X-ray satellites caught it; in 1992 its star's orbit showed the dark companion had to be a black hole, the surest case then known. Its star, a little over half the Sun's mass and swollen to five times its width, fills the space where its gravity rules, and gas spills off its tip into a disc. Most of the time the disc is cool and faint and stops far short of the hole. Every few decades it floods inwards and the system flares (1938, 1989, 2015), briefly one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky. A third star goes round the pair at least 3,500 AU out.

systems.name: MAXI J1820+070
systems.title: Black hole spinning on a tilted axis
systems.about: Burst into view in March 2018, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky for months, found by Japan's MAXI camera on the space station (an earlier outburst shows on photographs from 1934). Its star, an orange subgiant half the Sun's mass, spills gas into a disc round the black hole. Its jets, which point along the black hole's spin, are tipped at least 40 degrees from its orbit: the black hole spins on a tilted axis, probably since it formed. Quiet since 2019.

systems.name: GRS 1915+105
systems.title: Black hole whose jets seemed to outrun light
systems.about: Found in 1992 by the GRANAT satellite, and for 26 years one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, flickering in a dozen patterns no other source shows. In 1994 its jets became the first in our galaxy seen to move apparently faster than light: an illusion of blobs coming towards us at ~0.8 of light's speed. It's fed by a red giant on a 34-day orbit, the widest known for a black hole fed this way. Since 2019 dense gas near the black hole has hidden it in X-rays, and it feeds less; it still flares in radio.

systems.name: OGLE-2011-BLG-0462
systems.title: Lone black hole, found by the starlight it bent
systems.about: The only black hole known with nothing going round it. In 2011 it drifted almost exactly in front of a star 23,000 light-years away, towards the Galaxy's centre. Its gravity bent the star's light into two images too close together to tell apart, together 400 times brighter than the star alone at the peak, in July 2011; it brightened and faded over a year and a half. Hubble watched the star's image shift by up to 2 thousandths of an arcsecond, pulled aside by the bending, and from that shift and the brightening's timing came its mass: about 7 Suns, with no light of its own. Announced as a black hole in 2022; a rival analysis then gave 1.6 to 4.4 Suns (perhaps a neutron star), but with more Hubble data every analysis now gives a black hole. It moves at about 51 km/s against the stars round it, faster than almost all of them: probably kicked when it formed.

systems.name: Omega Centauri's black hole
systems.title: Medium-sized black hole at the heart of a star cluster
systems.about: Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's biggest globular cluster (about 4 million Suns of stars), is probably the stripped core of a small galaxy the Milky Way swallowed. In 2024, combing more than 500 Hubble images taken over 20 years, astronomers found seven stars within 3 arcseconds of its centre moving at 66 to 113 km/s: faster than the cluster's escape speed there (62 km/s). Stars that fast should leave the centre within a thousand years and then the cluster, so something unseen must hold them: a black hole of at least 8,200 Suns, and in the discoverers' models about 40,000. It's the nearest medium-sized black hole candidate, and after Sgr A* the second black hole with individual stars seen moving round it. Not everyone agrees: a rival analysis, with the cluster's pulsars, finds the centre's dark mass is better explained by many ordinary black holes spread over the core, leaving room for at most 6,000 Suns in one. No light from anything falling in has been seen.

systems.name: A0620-00
systems.title: One of the nearest black holes, fed by an orange dwarf
systems.about: Flared in August 1975, for weeks the brightest X-ray source in the sky; an earlier outburst shows on photographs from 1917. In 1986 its star's orbit showed the unseen companion was far too heavy for a neutron star, making it one of the first black holes of a star found, and still one of the nearest known. Its orange dwarf, under half the Sun's mass, goes round it every 7.75 hours, filling the space where its own gravity rules; gas spills off it into a faint disc. The orbit is slowly shrinking, faster than gravitational waves alone would make it.

systems.name: GRO J1655-40
systems.title: Black hole with jets near light's speed and an enriched star
systems.about: Found in July 1994 by the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory; weeks later radio images showed jets shooting out both ways at over 90% of light's speed, after GRS 1915+105 the second source in our galaxy seen to do so. Its star, a yellow-white subgiant over twice the Sun's mass, goes round the black hole every 2.6 days, and its surface is rich in oxygen, magnesium and other elements: debris from the supernova that made the black hole. It flared again in 1996 and 2005.

systems.name: 4U 1543-475
systems.title: Black hole with a hot white star, seen nearly face on
systems.about: One of the first X-ray novae, caught by the Uhuru satellite in 1971; it flared again in 1984, 1992, 2002 and 2021, the last time brighter than ever, perhaps feeding beyond the Eddington limit. Unlike most black holes fed this way, its star is a hot white A-type star over twice the Sun's mass. We see the orbit nearly face on, tilted only 21 degrees, so the star's speed towards and away from us is small and the masses took long to pin down.

systems.name: XTE J1550-564
systems.title: Black hole whose jets were seen slowing for years
systems.about: Found by the RXTE satellite in September 1998 in one of the brightest, most violent outbursts recorded, with radio blobs thrown out at most of light's speed. In 2000 Chandra caught its jets in X-rays: two knots moving out east and west, still glowing years later and slowing as they ploughed into the gas round it, the first X-ray jets resolved from a black hole fed by a star. Its orange subgiant goes round it every 37 hours. The jets point along the orbit's axis, so its spin is aligned with the orbit.

systems.name: V4641 Sagittarii
systems.title: Black hole with a blue giant, flaring within hours
systems.about: In September 1999 it flared from 14th to 9th magnitude, bright enough for binoculars, and faded again within a couple of hours, one of the fastest outbursts seen. Its star is a blue giant of nearly three Suns, far heavier and brighter than most black holes' companions, and it outshines the faint disc. It has flared every few years since, most recently in 2024. Its radio jet seems to point nearly at us, far from the orbit's axis, and in 2024 observatories found the highest-energy gamma rays from it of any such system, from a cloud stretching hundreds of light-years.

systems.name: GRS 1124-684
systems.title: Nova Muscae: a black hole on a shrinking orbit
systems.about: Flared in January 1991, caught by the Ginga and GRANAT satellites as one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, and in visible light by telescopes as a nova of 13th magnitude. Its orange dwarf, under a Sun's mass, goes round the black hole every 10.4 hours on an orbit that is shrinking fast, far faster than gravitational waves alone would make it. Since about 2003 it has been flickering more in visible light, its disc outshining the star.

systems.name: XTE J1118+480
systems.title: Black hole above the Galaxy's plane, on a four-hour orbit
systems.about: Found by RXTE in March 2000, high above the Milky Way's plane in Ursa Major where little gas or dust hides it, so it was watched across the spectrum from radio to X-rays; it stayed faint, never entering the bright soft state. Its small red dwarf whips round the black hole every 4.1 hours, one of the shortest orbits known for a black hole, and the orbit is shrinking much faster than expected. An earlier outburst, in 1927, shows on old photographs; another came in 2005.

systems.name: XTE J1859+226
systems.title: Black hole weighed by its X-ray flicker
systems.about: Found by RXTE in October 1999 in Vulpecula, and seen again in 2021, when the Zwicky Transient Facility caught it brightening in visible light. During its 1999 outburst its X-rays flickered in three rhythms at once; read as orbits and wobbles of gas close to the black hole, they give its mass and spin, 7.85 Suns, matching the mass from its star's orbit. Its orange dwarf goes round it every 6.6 hours.

systems.name: MAXI J1305-704
systems.title: Black hole seen nearly edge on, its X-rays dipping
systems.about: Found by MAXI on the space station in April 2012. While it was bright its X-rays dipped every few hours as clumps of gas at the disc's rim passed in front, so we see the disc nearly edge on. Its star's orbit, measured in quiescence in 2021, confirmed a black hole. It lies far below the Galaxy's plane and moves fast, probably kicked when the black hole formed.

systems.name: Swift J1727.8-1613
systems.title: Black hole with the longest resolved jet of its kind
systems.about: Found by the Swift satellite in August 2023; it became one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky and stayed in outburst for ten months. Radio telescopes saw its jet stretching north and south, the longest continuous jet yet resolved from a black hole fed by a star, and blobs thrown out along it again and again. Once it faded in 2024, its star's orbit confirmed a black hole of at least 3 Suns, moving fast, probably kicked when it formed.

systems.name: GX 339-4
systems.title: The most restless black hole, flaring every few years
systems.about: Found in 1972, it has flared more than 20 times since, every two or three years, each time running through the states black holes fed by a star go through: from a faint hard state with a steady jet to a bright soft disc and back. Much of what is known about how these discs and jets change comes from watching it. Its star is so faint against the disc that its orbit was only measured in 2017, from infrared spectra taken while the system was quiet.

systems.name: GS 1354-64
systems.title: Black hole beyond the Galaxy's far side
systems.about: Flared in 1987, seen by Ginga, and again in 1997 and 2015; an X-ray source seen there in 1971 was probably it too. Its star is a yellow giant on a 2.5-day orbit, and its brightness and the system's speed away from us put it about 25 kpc away (80,000 light-years or more), beyond the far side of the Milky Way's disc, one of the most distant black holes of its kind known in our galaxy. Gaia's parallax, though uncertain, would put it far closer; the two disagree.

systems.name: XTE J1650-500
systems.title: Black hole with smeared iron light
systems.about: Found by RXTE in September 2001 in Ara. Its X-rays showed the glow of iron smeared out into a broad skewed line, light from gas whirling round very close to the black hole and bent by its gravity: one of the first strong signs that black holes of stars spin. Its orange dwarf goes round it every 7.7 hours; even in quiescence the disc gives most of the light.

systems.title: The quietest black hole in X-rays
systems.about: Flared in April 1988, found by Japan's Ginga satellite, and quiet ever since. systems.title: Perhaps the lightest black hole known
systems.about: Found in August 1992 by the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory, for weeks one of the brightest sources in the sky in hard X-rays. Its red dwarf circles every 5.1 hours.
